items.text: Identifying the intent of a citation in scientiﬁc papers (e.g., background information, use of methods, comparing results) is critical for machine reading of individual publications and automated analysis of the scientiﬁc literature.
items.why: Explains why classifying citation intent is important.
items.plain: Classifying why a scientific paper cites another source helps computers read and analyze academic literature.

items.text: We propose structural scaffolds, a multitask model to incorporate structural information of scientiﬁc papers into citations for effective classiﬁcation of citation intents.
items.plain: We present structural scaffolds, a multi-task machine learning model that uses a paper's structural information to classify citation intents.

items.text: Our model achieves a new state-ofthe-art on an existing ACL anthology dataset (ACL-ARC) with a 13.3% absolute increase in F1 score, without relying on external linguistic resources or hand-engineered features as done in existing methods.
items.why: States the main result on the existing benchmark.
items.plain: Our model sets a new best result on the ACL-ARC benchmark dataset with a 13.3% absolute gain in F1 score without using manual features or outside linguistic tools.

items.text: In addition, we introduce a new dataset of citation intents (Sci- Cite) which is more than ﬁve times larger and covers multiple scientiﬁc domains compared with existing datasets.
items.plain: We also release SciCite, a citation intent dataset that is over five times larger than older datasets and covers multiple scientific fields.

items.text: Existing models for this problem are feature-based, modeling the citation context with respect to a set of predeﬁned handengineered features (such as linguistic patterns or cue phrases) and ignoring other signals that could improve prediction.
items.why: Identifies the gap in previous models.
items.plain: Older methods rely on human-designed rules and patterns, missing other helpful signals.

items.text: In particular, we propose two auxiliary tasks as structural scaffolds to improve citation intent prediction:1 (1) predicting the section title in which the citation occurs and (2) predicting whether a sentence needs a citation.
items.why: Defines the two specific auxiliary tasks used.
items.plain: We use two helper tasks: predicting which paper section contains a citation and predicting whether a sentence requires a citation.

items.text: On two datasets, we show that the proposed neural scaffold model outperforms existing methods by large margins.
items.why: Summarizes the overall experimental finding across datasets.
items.plain: Our neural scaffold model outperforms previous approaches by a wide margin across two datasets.

items.text: Our contributions are: (i) we propose a neural scaffold framework for citation intent classiﬁcation to incorporate into citations knowledge from structure of scientiﬁc papers; (ii) we achieve a new state-of-the-art of 67.9% F1 on the ACL- ARC citations benchmark, an absolute 13.3% increase over the previous state-of-the-art (Jurgens et al., 2018); and (iii) we introduce SciCite, a new dataset of citation intents which is at least ﬁve times as large as existing datasets and covers a variety of scientiﬁc domains.
items.plain: Our paper introduces a structural neural scaffold model, sets a new top F1 score of 67.9% on the ACL-ARC dataset (a 13.3% increase), and releases the larger SciCite dataset.

items.text: A key point for our proposed scaffolds is that they do not need any additional manual annotation as labels for these tasks occur naturally in scientiﬁc writing.
items.why: Highlights a major advantage of the method.
items.plain: The helper tasks do not require manual labeling because their labels occur naturally in written papers.

items.text: In addition, to address the limited scope and size of this dataset, we introduce SciCite, a new dataset of citation intents that addresses multiple scientiﬁc domains and is more than ﬁve times larger than ACL-ARC.
items.why: Describes the role of SciCite relative to existing data.
items.plain: To overcome the small size and limited domain scope of ACL-ARC, we created SciCite, which covers multiple domains and is over five times larger.

items.text: The best result is achieved when we also add ELMo vectors (Peters et al., 2018) to the input representations in ‘BiLSTM-Attn w/ ELMo + both scaffolds’, achieving an F1 of 67.9, a major improvement from the previous state-of-the-art results of Jurgens et al. (2018) 54.6 (∆=13.3).
items.why: Gives the primary headline performance metric and comparison.
items.plain: Combining both auxiliary tasks with ELMo embeddings gives an F1 score of 67.9%, outperforming the previous best result of 54.6% by 13.3 points.

items.text: We note that the scaffold tasks provide major contributions on top of the ELMo-enabled baseline (∆=13.6), demonstrating the efﬁcacy of using structural scaffolds for citation intent prediction.
items.why: Shows the isolated impact of the scaffolds.
items.plain: Adding the scaffold tasks provided a 13.6-point gain over the ELMo baseline alone.

items.text: We note that these results were obtained without using hand-curated features or additional linguistic resources as used in Jurgens et al. (2018).
items.why: Reiterates that no feature engineering was needed.
items.plain: These top results were achieved without hand-crafted features or extra linguistic tools.

items.text: Table 4 shows the main results on SciCite dataset, where we see similar patterns.
items.why: Confirms the performance trend on the new dataset.
items.plain: Results on the SciCite dataset show similar performance improvements.

items.text: In this work, we show that structural properties related to scientiﬁc discourse can be effectively used to inform citation intent classiﬁcation.
items.plain: Structural properties of scientific writing can improve automatic classification of citation intents.

items.text: Our model achieves state-of-the-art result (F1 score of 67.9%) on the ACL-ARC dataset with 13.3 absolute increase over the best previous results.
items.plain: Our model achieves a state-of-the-art F1 score of 67.9% on ACL-ARC, a 13.3-point absolute increase.

items.text: We demonstrate that carefully chosen auxiliary tasks that are inherently relevant to a main task can be leveraged to improve the performance on the main task.
items.why: Summarizes the general conclusion about auxiliary tasks.
items.plain: Relevant auxiliary tasks can be designed to boost performance on a main prediction task.
